new_statements.quote: [p. 4] C) RÈGLES GÉNÉRALES 9. Chaque mot se prononce absolument comme il est écrit. 10. L'accent tonique se place toujours sur l'avant-dernière syllabe. — [p. 10] C) GENERAL RULES 9. Every word is to be read exactly as written, there are no silent letters. 10. The accent falls on the last syllable but one, (penultimate). — [German] 10. Der Accent fällt immer auf die vorletzte Silbe. — [Russian] 10. Удареніе всегда находится на предпослѣднемъ слогѣ. — [Polish] 10. Akcent pada zawsze na przedostatnią zgłoskę.
new_statements.translation: 10. The tonic accent is always placed on the next-to-last syllable. (English version is original.) German/Russian/Polish: The accent always falls on the penultimate syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable (penultimate vowel; j and ŭ are glides, not syllabic) of every polysyllabic word, without lexical exceptions; when the noun ending -o is elided with an apostrophe (poetry), stress stays on the same, now final, syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Fundamento says nothing. Wennergren PMEG 15.5 §2.2 pp. 30-31: optional weaker 'kromakcentoj' may appear in long words, especially compounds, either rhythmically or on the stressed vowel of the first member (màtenmánĝo / matènmánĝo); 'Regulo ekzistas nur pri ĉefakcentoj. Kromakcentoj estas ĉiam libervolaj' (a rule exists only for main stress; secondary stresses are always optional and may be placed anywhere). Gledhill 2000 p. 33 likewise reports an optional pretonic accent on the first element of compounds (/vápor'Sípo/).
new_statements.exceptions: None in the norm. PMEG §2.1 p. 23: apostrophized nouns keep stress on the original penult, now final (taksí', revolvér', metró'); §2.2 p. 31: contrastive emphasis may override the rule (màlbona with strongest stress on mal-), called natural and permissible; unemphatic function words (antaŭ, ili, kiel, esti, havi) are often unaccented in running speech. Gledhill p. 36: L1-influenced deviations (French speakers /internatsiá/, English /internátsia/) and leftward shift in connected speech (/áliel/, /áNkoraw/) occur but are deviations from the norm.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the (orthographic/grammatical) word including its grammatical ending; monosyllables unstressed or stressed by phrase emphasis; PMEG describes realization as greater loudness, often with length and higher pitch, with no obligatory phonetic correlate.
new_statements.identity_note: Standard Esperanto as defined by the Fundamento (1905) and described by PMEG; no dialect issue. Gledhill and PMEG note L1-influenced deviations and optional secondary/contrastive stress in compounds, but the norm and general usage are uniform.

sources.citation: Kellerman, Ivy. 1910. A Complete Grammar of Esperanto. Chicago: D. C. Heath & Co. (Project Gutenberg #7787 text)
sources.note: §8 'Accent': 'Words of more than one syllable are accented upon the syllable before the last, as TA-blo, a-GRA-bla, sus-PEK-ti.' §280b: when final -o is elided in poetry 'The original accent of the noun remains unchanged' (kor', rozet').

sources.citation: Wennergren, Bertilo. 2024. PMEG: Plena Manlibro de Esperanta Gramatiko, versio 15.5 (21 Junio 2024). bertilow.com/pmeg (CC BY-SA 4.0). PDF, 754 pp.
sources.note: §2.1 'Akcento', p. 23: 'La akcento estas ĉiam sur la antaŭlasta vokalo' with examples táblo, neníam, familío, metróo, anstátaŭ, málpli; Ŭ and J are not vowels; apostrophe-elided -o counts as an unpronounced vowel so stress stays (taksí', revolvér'). §2.2 'Kromakcentoj', pp. 30-31: optional weaker secondary accents in long/compound words (matènmánĝo or màtenmánĝo), 'Regulo ekzistas nur pri ĉefakcentoj. Kromakcentoj estas ĉiam libervolaj'; contrastive stress may override (màlbona); 'Foresto de akcento' p. 31: unemphatic function words (antaŭ, ili, kiel, esti) often carry no accent in practice.

sources.citation: Gledhill, Christopher. 1998 (2nd ed. 2000). The Grammar of Esperanto: A corpus-based description. (Languages of the World/Materials 190.) München: Lincom Europa. HAL author version hal-01220008, 152 pp.
sources.note: §1.3 Pronunciation, p. 36 (HAL version): 'The stress pattern of Esperanto is theoretically fixed to an accent on the penultimate syllable in all polysyllabic words (i.e. Rule 10..). Hence granda is pronounced /gránda/, usually with a correspondingly slight lengthening of the vowel.' Notes pretonic accent on first element of compounds (/vápor'Sípo/, p. 33), L1-influenced deviations (French /internatsiá/), leftward shift in connected speech (/áliel/, /áNkoraw/), and Kalocsay's remarks on /líbertémpo/.
